problem.statement: Standard memory profilers (dotMemory, ANTS, SciTech, VS diagnostics, dotnet-dump/gcroot) show that memory is retained or growing — or fail to reveal it despite low managed usage — but don't trace the ownership/reference path back to the specific code responsible, leaving developers unable to pinpoint and fix the leak.

persona.primary: WPF/legacy .NET desktop developer maintaining a WinForms or hybrid WinForms/WPF production app

context.situation: Developers maintaining legacy WinForms/WPF .NET applications hit production memory leaks or OOM crashes after hours of runtime, run a profiler that confirms objects are retained, but get stuck because the tool doesn't explain who is holding the reference (DI scopes, event subscriptions, async continuations, third-party controls, XAML bindings).

current_workarounds: Manually walking GC roots with dotnet-dump dumpheap/gcroot commands
Isolating the leak by commenting out XAML elements/bindings one at a time
Speculatively implementing IDisposable and manually nulling fields without confirming the actual cause
Switching APIs (BeginInvoke vs InvokeAsync, WinForms control vs WPF equivalent) to sidestep the leak without understanding it
Posting full source code publicly asking strangers to find the bug
Attaching the Visual Studio Remote Debugger directly to a production process
Manually tracking DI lifetime scopes/instances in a dictionary to force disposal
existing_substitutes: Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools / Remote Debugger

possible_wedges.offer: Ingest a memory dump or profiler snapshot and produce a plain-English ownership/root-cause chain report tuned to common WinForms/WPF leak patterns (DI scopes, WeakEventManager, Dispatcher, static events, virtualized ItemsControl/ListView).
A dotnet-dump wrapper that automates gcroot analysis across suspect types and outputs a ranked, annotated ownership report for use against production dumps or in CI.
Send-us-your-dump paid audit: an expert traces the ownership chain and delivers a root-cause report for legacy WinForms/WPF teams without in-house profiling expertise.

risks: All evidence is from public Q&A/bug trackers, not paying customers; commercial_intent signals are consistently low (0.05-0.15)
Root causes are highly varied (DI containers, event wiring, async/Dispatcher, third-party control internals, LINQ internals) so a tool needs broad pattern coverage to be reliably useful
Target users are already technically resourceful (using dotnet-dump, dotMemory) raising the bar to add value over existing free/paid profilers
Several leaks trace into third-party control internals (Telerik, Syncfusion, DevExpress, Krypton) that a tool can't fully instrument without vendor-level access
No evidence of anyone explicitly offering to pay; commitment signals are near zero across the cluster

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: Legacy .NET/WPF developers who've hit a wall with existing profilers (can see retention but not ownership) will pay for a fast, expert root-cause diagnosis of their leak.
cheapest_experiment.input: A memory dump or profiler snapshot plus a description of the symptom, submitted by a developer stuck on an unexplained leak (e.g. sourced from relevant Stack Overflow/GitHub issue threads).
cheapest_experiment.output: A written ownership/root-cause chain report identifying the exact code path or object holding the reference.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: Developer pays a flat fee (e.g. $150-300) upfront, or explicitly agrees to pay before the diagnosis is delivered.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: At least 3 of 10 developers contacted via relevant leak-debugging threads agree to pay for the diagnosis.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Fewer than 1 of 10 contacted convert, or all responses ask for free help despite the paid offer.
